blocks.text: Model introduction

“Good morning. My name is Dr ____. I understand you are considering the contraceptive implant. I would like to discuss your pregnancy-prevention goals, medical history and any medicines you take. I will explain how the implant works, its benefits and possible side effects, and what insertion and removal involve. You can ask questions at any time, and the decision will be yours. Is that alright?”

blocks.text: A pelvic examination and routine laboratory tests are not generally required before implant insertion in an otherwise eligible patient.
A. Single-rod etonogestrel implant
Example: Nexplanon.

items.text: Contains etonogestrel.
Inserted subdermally in the upper arm.
Commonly licensed for up to three years in many jurisdictions; some current product guidance permits longer use.
Radiopaque versions can be located using X-ray-based imaging when necessary.

blocks.text: B. Two-rod levonorgestrel implant
Example: Jadelle.

items.text: Contains levonorgestrel.
Consists of two flexible rods inserted under the skin.
Commonly licensed for up to five years.
Removal involves locating and removing both rods.

blocks.text: Exam point: the licensed duration depends on the specific implant, jurisdiction and current product information. Do not tell every patient that all implants last the same number of years. Check the product in use and the applicable guidance.

blocks.title: The implant prevents pregnancy primarily through:

items.text: Suppression of ovulation: progestogen inhibits the hormonal events required for ovulation.
Thickening of cervical mucus: sperm passage through the cervix becomes more difficult.
Endometrial changes: the endometrium becomes thinner.

blocks.text: The implant is highly effective because it does not depend on the user remembering a daily tablet.
It is not an abortifacient and does not terminate an established pregnancy.
The implant is among the most effective reversible contraceptive methods, with a first-year pregnancy rate below one per 100 users.

items.text: Very high contraceptive effectiveness.

No oestrogen.
Convenience for women who prefer discreet, long-acting contraception.
No need for a pelvic examination for routine insertion.
Ability to discontinue at any time through removal by a trained clinician.

blocks.text: It does not protect against sexually transmitted infections. Condoms should be offered when STI protection is needed.

blocks.text: The bleeding pattern may change throughout the duration of use. It is not possible to predict reliably which pattern an individual patient will experience.
Explain this before insertion, because unexpected bleeding is a common reason for discontinuation.

blocks.text: A history of migraine with aura, hypertension or previous VTE does not automatically exclude the implant; it may be suitable when oestrogen-containing contraception is not.
The implant must be inserted and removed by a clinician trained in the specific device.

The following is an examination framework for a trained clinician using the appropriate device instructions. In practice, insertion must follow the manufacturer's current instructions and local clinical protocols.

items.text: Confirm the indication and medical eligibility.
Exclude pregnancy when reasonably possible.
Explain the procedure, risks, benefits and alternatives.
Obtain informed consent.
Confirm the implant type and expiry date of the device.
Check for medication interactions.
Explain the expected bleeding changes and aftercare.
Position the patient comfortably with the non-dominant arm appropriately supported.

blocks.text: For a single-rod etonogestrel implant, the recommended site is on the inner aspect of the upper arm, over the triceps region, according to the manufacturer's anatomical landmarks.
The implant should be placed subdermally, avoiding the neurovascular structures in the medial upper arm.
OSCE safety point: incorrect or excessively deep insertion increases the risk of neurovascular injury and difficult removal.

content_groups.group_title: When does the implant become effective?

blocks.text: This depends on the timing of insertion and the method used previously.

For an etonogestrel implant, insertion within the first five days of menstrual bleeding generally provides immediate contraceptive protection. When inserted later, additional contraception is generally recommended for seven days, unless existing contraceptive coverage or specific clinical circumstances alter the advice.

Postpartum insertion, switching methods and recent unprotected intercourse require individual assessment. If pregnancy cannot reasonably be excluded, follow the relevant quick-start and follow-up guidance rather than automatically delaying every method.
Removal should be performed by a trained clinician using the device-specific technique.

blocks.text: Features may include increasing redness, warmth, pain, swelling, discharge or fever.

subsections.subsection_title: 14. Common examiner questions and model answers

blocks.text: Q1. What is the mechanism of action of the contraceptive implant?
It suppresses ovulation, thickens cervical mucus and produces endometrial changes. Suppression of ovulation and thickening of cervical mucus are the key mechanisms.
Q2. What is the most important adverse effect to discuss before insertion?
Unpredictable bleeding, including spotting, prolonged bleeding, infrequent bleeding or amenorrhoea.
Q3. Does the implant cause permanent infertility?
No. Fertility generally returns rapidly after removal.
Q4. What should you do if an implant is non-palpable?
Confirm the device and history, arrange appropriate localisation, and refer to an experienced clinician. Never attempt blind removal.
Q5. Which medicines can reduce implant effectiveness?
Enzyme-inducing medicines such as carbamazepine, phenytoin, rifampicin and rifabutin are important examples.
Q6. Is the implant suitable for a woman who has never given birth?
Yes. Nulliparity alone is not a contraindication.
Q7. Does the implant protect against STIs?
No. Condoms should be offered when STI protection is needed.
Q8. What are the key steps in safe insertion?
Confirm eligibility and consent, use aseptic technique and the device-specific method, ensure correct subdermal placement, palpate the implant, document insertion and provide aftercare advice.
Q9. What would you do if a patient requests removal because of bleeding?
Assess the bleeding and exclude other causes, discuss treatment if desired, and respect her request for removal. Arrange alternative contraception if she wishes to continue pregnancy prevention.
